Outputs still need to be evaluated no matter how good the prompt is.
Prompts can reduce some bias but cannot guarantee that it never appears.

questions.stem: A company calls InvokeModel with a guardrail whose prompt attack filter is set to block, and the filter strength is high. Testing shows that user-typed jailbreak attempts still reach the model. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Prompt attack filters work only on model responses and never on user prompts
The user input in the request is not wrapped in the guardrail's input tags
Jailbreaks are detected only after the model has already generated its answer
Guardrails cannot be applied to InvokeModel calls, only to the Converse API
questions.explanation: With InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream, the user input must be enclosed in the guardrail's input tags. Without the tags, prompt attacks in that input are not filtered.
whyWrong: The prompt attack filter is designed to evaluate user prompts for attacks such as jailbreaks.
The filter evaluates the tagged input before the model is invoked.
Guardrails can be used with InvokeModel when the input tags are applied.

questions.stem: A company's assistant summarizes web pages and can also send email through a connected tool. Testing shows that a page can hide text telling the assistant to email private data to an outsider. Which action BEST limits the damage if such an instruction gets through?
options: Raise the model temperature so hidden instructions are less likely to be followed
Ask users to read each summary after the assistant has already finished the work
Move the assistant to a larger foundation model with a longer context window
Restrict the tool's role to the minimum permissions that the task requires
questions.explanation: Hidden instructions in untrusted content are indirect prompt injection or hijacking. Applying least privilege to what the assistant can do limits the harm even when an injection succeeds; guardrails and input validation help reduce the attempts.
whyWrong: Temperature controls randomness and gives no protection against injected instructions.
Reviewing the summary after the email is sent cannot undo the action.
A larger model or longer context does not stop it from following injected instructions.

questions.stem: During a fine-tuning job, the training loss keeps falling, but the loss on the validation dataset starts to rise after the third epoch. What does this indicate, and what is a sensible response?
options: Underfitting, so increase the number of epochs for the next run
Overfitting, so reduce the epochs or stop training earlier
Data drift, so replace the model with a much larger one
Underfitting, so set the learning rate to its highest allowed value
questions.explanation: Falling training loss with rising validation loss means the model is memorizing the training data, which is overfitting. Fewer epochs or early stopping on validation loss is the usual remedy.
whyWrong: Underfitting would show poor results on both training and validation data, not a rising validation loss alone.
Data drift concerns changing production data after deployment, not a training-time loss pattern.
Rising validation loss is not underfitting, and a very high learning rate can make training unstable.

questions.stem: A team fine-tunes a model on only 400 labeled examples. At the default settings the model barely changes. Following AWS guidance on hyperparameters, what should the team adjust first?
options: Increase the number of epochs, since smaller datasets need more passes to converge
Decrease the epochs to one, because small datasets always converge faster than large ones
Raise the learning rate to its maximum, which AWS recommends for the fastest convergence
Swap in a larger unlabeled corpus and run continued pre-training instead of fine-tuning
questions.explanation: Each epoch processes the whole training dataset once. Smaller datasets generally need more epochs to converge, while a higher learning rate is less desirable because it can make training unstable.
whyWrong: Fewer epochs would make a small dataset under-train even more.
A very high learning rate can cause unstable training, so it is not the recommended first change.
That abandons fine-tuning and does not fix under-training on the labeled data the team already has.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about transfer learning are correct? (Choose two.)
options: It requires the new task to use exactly the same data as the original task
It reuses a model trained on one task as the start for a related task
It needs less data and compute than training a custom model from scratch
It trains a model from random weights without using any pretrained knowledge at all
It removes the need for any data from the new task before the model is used
questions.explanation: Transfer learning adapts a model already trained on one task to a new, related task, which typically needs less data and compute than starting from scratch. It still uses data from the new task.
whyWrong: The new task and data differ from the original; that is the point of adapting the model.
That describes training from scratch, which transfer learning avoids.
Some data from the new task is still used to adapt the model.

questions.stem: A team labeled 8,000 support messages with a single contractor for fine-tuning. Spot checks show many wrong labels, and the contractor's personal preferences seem to skew the categories. Which step BEST improves label quality?
options: Send each item to several annotators and consolidate their answers into one label
Let the model being fine-tuned relabel the data and treat its output as ground truth
Add more epochs so that the model learns to ignore the incorrect labels
Keep the labels as they are but drop the validation dataset so that errors are not measured
questions.explanation: A model is only as accurate as the labeled data it learns from. Consensus labeling offsets individual error and bias, and auditing labels adds quality assurance.
whyWrong: A model's own output is not independent ground truth and would reinforce its mistakes.
More epochs make the model fit the wrong labels harder, not ignore them.
Dropping the validation data hides the problem and does not fix any of the labels.

questions.stem: A team is preparing a fine-tuning job in Amazon Bedrock and wants to measure loss on examples that the model does not train on. What should the team prepare?
options: A second copy of the training file to use as the validation data
A set of unlabeled documents stored in a separate Amazon S3 bucket
A much larger training file so that the job can run for more epochs
A separate validation dataset in the same JSONL format
questions.explanation: Customization jobs take JSONL training data and, where supported, a separate JSONL validation dataset. Validation examples are held out so that loss on unseen data can be measured.
whyWrong: A copy contains the same examples the model trains on, so it cannot measure performance on unseen data.
Unlabeled documents do not match the prompt-and-completion records needed for validation.
More training data and epochs do not provide any held-out examples.

questions.stem: An online course provider adds an AI tutor to its lessons. The stated business goal is to keep learners engaged with their courses. Six weeks after launch, which measurement best shows whether the tutor meets this goal?
options: The hallucination rate of the tutor's answers in sampled chats
The average latency of tutor responses during peak study hours
Weekly active learners and lesson completion rates
The token cost per tutor session compared with the monthly budget
questions.explanation: User engagement, such as active user count, repeat usage and task completion, shows whether an application meets its business objective. Hallucination rate measures model quality, and latency and cost measure system health.
whyWrong: Hallucination rate measures answer quality, not whether learners stay engaged.
Latency is a system health metric; fast replies do not prove engagement.
Cost per session tracks spending efficiency, not learner engagement.

questions.stem: A company runs a conversational agent that streams its answers to users as they are generated. Which latency measure should be the key release gate for this agent?
options: Total completion time of a full multi-step task
Overnight throughput of batch workloads
Time to first token and inter-token latency
CPU utilization of the host running the agent
questions.explanation: Users of streaming conversational agents perceive responsiveness through time to first token and inter-token latency. End-to-end completion time matters most for task-oriented agents that return one result, and throughput matters most for batch.
whyWrong: Total task time is the primary measure for task-oriented agents that return a single result.
Batch throughput matters for asynchronous workflows, not interactive streaming.
CPU utilization is an infrastructure signal that does not show what users experience.

questions.stem: A travel-booking agent usually gives correct final answers, but its traces show it often calls the wrong tool first and then recovers, which adds cost and delay. The team wants an evaluation signal that catches this problem directly. Which measure should it add?
options: BLEU scores comparing final answers with reference answers
Tool selection accuracy for each step the agent takes
Average CPU utilization of the agent's runtime hosts
User ratings of the final answer in each session
questions.explanation: Agent quality signals include tool selection and parameter accuracy, which judge each step of the run. Scores on the final answer miss a wrong tool call that the agent later recovers from.
whyWrong: BLEU scores only the final text, so it misses wrong tool calls along the way.
CPU utilization is an infrastructure metric and says nothing about the agent's choices.
Ratings judge the final outcome, which is usually correct here.

questions.stem: An Amazon Bedrock flow chains a prompt node, a knowledge base node, and an AWS Lambda function. Some final answers are wrong, and the team must find which step introduces the error. What should the team do?
options: Turn on the flow trace to inspect each node's inputs and outputs
Score only the final answers against references with a BLEU metric
Lower the temperature on the prompt node and rerun the whole flow
Enable Provisioned Throughput for the model behind the prompt node
questions.explanation: A flow trace shows the inputs to and outputs from each node, so the team can follow the path and find the step that leads to the unexpected outcome. End-to-end scores only show that the result is wrong.
whyWrong: A score on final answers cannot show which node caused the error.
Changing a parameter guesses at a fix without locating the faulty step.
Reserved capacity affects throughput, not the correctness of any step.

questions.stem: A team wants to stop agent releases that lower the share of tasks the agent completes or that push the cost per task above a set limit. What should the team do?
options: Look over the dashboards by hand after each release reaches production
Check task completion rate and cost per task as gates in the deployment pipeline
Report only the average CPU utilization of the infrastructure that hosts the agent
Wait for customers to complain and then roll back to the previous version
questions.explanation: Success criteria such as task completion rate and cost per task can be checked against a curated evaluation set in CI/CD, so that releases which miss a target are blocked before reaching users.
whyWrong: Manual review after release detects regressions only after users are affected.
CPU utilization is an infrastructure metric that says nothing about task completion or cost per task.
Customer complaints are a late, unreliable signal and the regression has already shipped.

questions.stem: A company's support agent dashboard tracks latency, errors, cost per interaction, and task completion. Leadership now asks whether customers actually value the agent and keep coming back to it. Which metrics should the team add?
options: Token spend broken down per session and per task
Tool invocation patterns across each agent session
Memory usage of the agent runtime during peak hours
User satisfaction ratings and repeat-usage rates
questions.explanation: Human-centric metrics such as satisfaction, trust, and re-engagement show whether the agent matters to users, which performance and cost metrics cannot show.
whyWrong: Token spend measures cost, not how users value the agent.
Tool patterns describe agent behavior, not user value.
Memory usage is an infrastructure signal, not a measure of user value.

questions.stem: A hardware retailer's assistant must decline requests for instructions that could lead to physical injury, such as mixing household cleaning chemicals. Which responsible AI dimension is the team addressing?
options: Fairness, which weighs the system's impact on different groups of stakeholders
Veracity and robustness, which keeps outputs correct even with unexpected inputs
Safety, which aims to prevent harmful system output and its misuse
Transparency, which helps stakeholders make informed choices about the system
questions.explanation: AWS defines safety as preventing harmful system output and misuse, which covers declining dangerous instructions. Fairness concerns impacts on groups, veracity and robustness concern correct outputs, and transparency concerns informed choices.
whyWrong: Fairness concerns how outcomes differ across groups, not blocking dangerous content.
Veracity and robustness concern correct outputs, not withholding harmful ones.
Transparency concerns informing stakeholders about the system, not blocking harmful output.

questions.stem: A travel assistant built on Amazon Bedrock must never show customers' booking codes, which follow the pattern BK- plus eight digits. The team wants any such code replaced with a placeholder in responses. Which guardrail configuration meets this?
options: A denied topic defined as any text that contains a booking code of this format
A word filter that lists each known booking code as an exact phrase
A sensitive information filter with a custom regex set to mask
A contextual grounding check with a high relevance threshold
questions.explanation: Sensitive information filters accept custom regex patterns and can mask matches in model responses. Denied topics and word filters are not suited to pattern-based entities.
whyWrong: Denied topics block subject areas, not text that matches a code pattern.
Word filters match exact words or phrases, so new codes would slip through.
Grounding and relevance checks do not detect or mask patterns.

questions.stem: A RAG assistant on Amazon Bedrock sometimes replies with accurate statements copied from the retrieved documents that do not answer what the customer asked. Which guardrail policy detects this?
options: A contextual grounding check using only a grounding threshold
A sensitive information filter set to block personal data
A word filter with a custom list of off-topic phrases
A contextual grounding check with a relevance threshold
questions.explanation: The relevance check flags responses that do not answer the user's query even when they are grounded in the source.
whyWrong: Such a reply is grounded in the source, so a grounding check alone would pass it.
This filter detects personal data, not off-topic answers.
A phrase list cannot capture an unbounded set of off-topic replies.

questions.stem: Visitors to a parts catalog type an exact part number and need the matching product page. A developer proposes adding a large language model to find it. Which choice best supports the company's sustainability goals?
options: Fine-tune a language model on the whole catalog so it memorizes every part number
Use a standard database or search lookup instead of generative AI
Use the largest available model to maximize answer accuracy
Keep a dedicated GPU endpoint running so responses are instant
questions.explanation: A simpler lookup achieves the same outcome with far fewer resources, so first ask whether generative AI is the right tool.
whyWrong: Fine-tuning consumes compute for a task that exact matching already solves.
The largest model uses the most energy for no added benefit here.
An always-on GPU endpoint wastes energy while idle.

questions.stem: A company is reviewing legal and business risks before launching a public generative AI feature. Which two risks should it include? (Choose two.)
options: Using a managed service transfers all legal responsibility for outputs to AWS
Biased outputs can create discrimination complaints and legal exposure
A larger context window removes the need to review outputs
Harmful or embarrassing outputs can damage customer trust in the brand
Prompts and completions are always used to retrain the base model
questions.explanation: Biased outputs can bring legal exposure, and harmful outputs can erode customer trust. Responsibility stays with the deploying company, and Bedrock does not use prompts to train base models.
whyWrong: The deploying company remains responsible for how it uses model output.
Review is still needed regardless of context window size.
Bedrock prompts and completions are not used to train base models.

questions.stem: A marketing agency will generate ad copy and images with a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock. Its legal team's top concern is third-party claims that the generated outputs infringe copyrights. Which choice most directly reduces the agency's exposure to this risk?
options: Use a generally available Amazon Nova model, whose outputs AWS covers with IP indemnity
Turn on model invocation logging so that every generated output is stored for later review
Use any third-party model on Bedrock, since AWS indemnifies the outputs of every model
Raise the temperature so that outputs are more original and less like existing works
questions.explanation: AWS offers uncapped intellectual property indemnity for outputs of generally available Amazon Nova models, protecting customers from third-party claims that those outputs infringe IP, including copyright. Logging and sampling settings do not address legal liability.
whyWrong: Logging records outputs but gives no protection against infringement claims.
The AWS indemnity described here covers generally available Amazon Nova outputs, not every provider's model.
Temperature changes randomness and offers no legal protection against claims.

questions.stem: A team labels photos with the emotion shown. All its annotators live in one region, and the trained model misreads expressions common elsewhere. What should the team do to improve the dataset?
options: Remove the misread examples from the training set so scores look better
Add annotators from varied backgrounds and use shared guidelines
Train longer on the existing labels until accuracy rises
Switch to a larger model with more layers
questions.explanation: Diverse annotators reduce blind spots in labels, making the dataset more representative.
whyWrong: Removing hard examples hides the gap and worsens representation.
More training on biased labels reinforces the bias.
A larger model does not fix unrepresentative labels.

questions.stem: A data scientist wants a more reliable estimate of how well a model generalizes by repeatedly training on part of the data and validating on the held-out part. Which technique does this?
options: K-fold cross-validation
Early stopping of the training run
L1 regularization of the model weights
Bagging with several parallel models
questions.explanation: K-fold cross-validation uses each data subset once as validation data and averages the scores, revealing overfitting.
whyWrong: Early stopping is a prevention method, not an estimate by repeated splits.
Regularization penalizes complexity during training; it estimates nothing.
Bagging combines models to reduce variance; it is not a validation scheme.

questions.stem: A lender tests its approval model by changing only an applicant's gender in otherwise identical records and checking whether the decision changes. Which approach is this?
options: K-fold cross-validation across several data splits
Random oversampling of the minority class in the training data
Counterfactual fairness testing of paired records
Hyperparameter tuning of the learning rate and batch size
questions.explanation: Swapping a sensitive characteristic and seeing whether the decision changes is counterfactual fairness testing.
whyWrong: Cross-validation estimates generalization, not group treatment.
Oversampling changes class balance; it does not test decisions.
Tuning hyperparameters improves training and does not test for bias.

questions.stem: A regulator asks why a complex model denied one specific applicant. Which output best answers the question?
options: The model's overall accuracy and error rate on a held-out test set
Feature attributions showing each input's effect on that decision
The training loss curve from the most recent training run
A list of the hyperparameters used during training
questions.explanation: Per-prediction feature attributions, such as Shapley values, explain the contribution of each input to an individual decision.
whyWrong: Overall accuracy describes the whole model, not one decision.
A loss curve shows training progress, not why a decision was made.
Hyperparameters describe configuration, not an individual outcome.

questions.stem: A lender's responsible AI team separates its transparency work from its explainability work. Which deliverable is mainly a transparency measure rather than an explanation of model outputs?
options: Feature attributions that show why one applicant received a particular score
Published notes on the model's intended uses, data sources and limitations
A partial dependence plot showing how income shifts predictions on average
A counterfactual showing the smallest change that would flip one decision
questions.explanation: AWS describes explainability as understanding and evaluating system outputs, and transparency as enabling stakeholders to make informed choices about engaging with the system. Documenting intended uses, data and limitations informs those choices; attributions, partial dependence and counterfactuals explain outputs.
whyWrong: Feature attributions explain an individual output, which is explainability.
A partial dependence plot explains how an input affects predictions.
A counterfactual explains what would change a specific decision.

questions.stem: Before choosing a model for a public question-answering tool, a governance team wants documented, comparable evidence for each candidate model on Amazon Bedrock: how often it produces harmful language and how often its answers are correct. The team has no prompt dataset of its own. Which two metrics should it select in an automatic model evaluation job with built-in datasets? (Choose two.)
options: Robustness, which measures how much answers change when prompts contain small typos
Toxicity, which scores generated responses for harmful content
Grounding, which checks responses against retrieved source passages
Accuracy, which compares responses with reference answers in the dataset
Latency, which measures how long each candidate model takes to respond
questions.explanation: Automatic model evaluation in Amazon Bedrock reports accuracy, robustness, and toxicity, with built-in datasets for each. Toxicity covers harmful content and accuracy covers correctness; robustness measures how output shifts under small perturbations such as typos.
whyWrong: Robustness measures sensitivity to minor input changes, not harm or correctness.
Grounding checks are a Guardrails runtime feature, not an automatic evaluation metric.
Latency is not one of the automatic evaluation metrics and says nothing about harm or correctness.

questions.stem: A bank's assistant on Amazon Bedrock uses a guardrail. Product owners want customers told clearly when a request cannot be answered. The security team warns that revealing which filter fired, and at what strength, would help attackers probe the guardrail. Which approach balances both concerns?
options: Return the full guardrail trace to customers so every block decision is explained
Turn the guardrail off for customer chats and add a general disclaimer instead
Show the blocked prompt back to the customer with the matched filter highlighted
Configure a custom blocked message that declines politely without filter details
questions.explanation: A guardrail includes messaging for blocked prompts and responses, and the team can replace the default text with its own. A clear, generic decline keeps users informed while withholding the filter details attackers could exploit, trading a little transparency for safety.
whyWrong: The trace shows which policies fired, which is the detail the security team wants withheld.
Removing the guardrail gives up safety entirely in exchange for a disclaimer.
Highlighting the matched filter tells attackers exactly what to change.

questions.stem: An Amazon Bedrock agent uses an action group backed by an AWS Lambda function that issues refunds. Security wants only that one agent to be able to invoke the function, not other agents or services in the account. What should the team configure?
options: A resource-based policy on the function that allows Bedrock with the agent's ARN as source
An identity-based policy for the developers that allows lambda:InvokeFunction on the function
A guardrail on the agent with a denied topic that covers refund requests from other agents
A customer managed AWS KMS key that encrypts the function's environment variables
questions.explanation: Amazon Bedrock invokes action group functions through a resource-based policy on the Lambda function. Allowing the Bedrock service principal with a source ARN condition for the specific agent limits invocation to that agent, which applies least privilege.
whyWrong: Developers' permissions do not control which service can call the function on the agent's behalf.
Guardrails filter content; they do not control who can invoke a Lambda function.
Encryption protects data at rest and does not restrict who invokes the function.

questions.stem: A company requires that every model inference call its developers make through Amazon Bedrock includes the approved guardrail. Requests without it must fail, whichever application sends them. Which approach enforces this?
options: Enable model invocation logging and review the logs weekly for missing guardrails
An IAM policy that denies inference unless the request names the approved guardrail
A system prompt in each application telling the model to apply the approved guardrail
A customer managed AWS KMS key that encrypts the approved guardrail's configuration
questions.explanation: The bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key lets an IAM policy deny Converse and InvokeModel requests that do not include the specified guardrail, so enforcement happens at authorization rather than in application code.
whyWrong: Logging and review find gaps after the fact; they do not make requests fail.
A guardrail is attached to the request; a prompt instruction cannot apply or enforce it.
Encrypting the guardrail protects it but does not force requests to use it.

questions.stem: A data lake table used to train a churn model holds customer behavior fields plus social security numbers and birth dates. Data scientists must query the table for training but must never see those two fields. Which solution meets this requirement?
options: Run Amazon Macie on the underlying Amazon S3 data to discover the sensitive fields
Encrypt the table's Amazon S3 objects with a customer managed AWS KMS key
Grant AWS Lake Formation permissions with a data filter that excludes the columns
Use AWS Glue DataBrew to profile the table and report its data quality issues
questions.explanation: Lake Formation data filters provide column-level security, so the data scientists can query the table while the excluded personal data never appears in their results.
whyWrong: Macie discovers and reports sensitive data; it does not restrict what a user can query.
Object encryption protects the whole object, so a reader with key access sees every field.
DataBrew profiles and prepares data; it does not enforce column-level access.

questions.stem: A regulated lender must prove that the dataset used to train a credit model was not altered or deleted for five years after training. No one, including administrators, may be able to change it during that time. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Enable S3 Versioning so every overwrite of the dataset creates a new version
Turn on CloudTrail data events to record every write to the dataset's bucket
Use an S3 Lifecycle rule that moves the dataset to S3 Glacier after 30 days
Store the dataset in S3 with Object Lock retention in compliance mode
questions.explanation: Object Lock stores objects as write-once-read-many. In compliance mode no user, including the root user, can overwrite or delete a locked version or shorten its retention, which supports data integrity requirements.
whyWrong: Versioning keeps old versions, but users with permission can still delete them.
CloudTrail records changes after they happen; it does not prevent them.
Moving data to S3 Glacier lowers cost but does not stop deletion or overwrite.

questions.stem: A company's Amazon Bedrock guardrail blocks prompts that contain customer card numbers, and model invocation logging is turned on. An audit later finds card numbers from the blocked prompts stored in plain text. What explains this, and what is a fix?
options: Invocation logging captured the blocked prompts; turn it off or keep them out of logs
The guardrail checked only model responses; apply it to user prompts as well
Rotating the log encryption key exposed old entries; stop rotating the KMS key
Amazon Macie copied the card numbers during a scan; turn off Macie data discovery
questions.explanation: Content blocked by guardrail policies still appears as plain text in model invocation logs when logging is enabled. Turning off invocation logging, or keeping that content out of the logs, closes the leak.
whyWrong: Guardrails evaluate user inputs as well as model responses, and this one already blocks prompts.
Rotating a KMS key does not decrypt or expose log data; the content was written by invocation logging.
Macie discovers and reports sensitive data; it does not copy it into new places.

questions.stem: An HR assistant uses RAG over the company's policy documents. When the retrieved passages do not cover a question, it still gives a confident, invented policy. Which change best grounds its answers?
options: Fine-tune the model on the policy documents each quarter
Tell it to answer only from the passages and to say when it does not know
Add a denied-topic guardrail that blocks policy questions
Add examples of confident answers so it sounds sure of every policy
questions.explanation: Grounding instructions limit the model to the retrieved content and let it say it does not know when the answer is missing, so it stops filling gaps with invented facts. Fine-tuning, blocking the topic and confident examples do not stop it inventing.
whyWrong: Fine-tuning bakes in older policy text and still lets the model invent answers when a topic is missing.
Blocking policy questions stops the assistant doing its job instead of grounding its answers.
Confident examples reinforce invented answers instead of letting it admit a gap.

questions.stem: A healthcare company subject to HIPAA must have a Business Associate Addendum with AWS before it processes protected health information in its AI workloads. Where can it review and accept this agreement?
options: AWS Config
AWS Artifact
AWS Trusted Advisor
Amazon Inspector
questions.explanation: AWS Artifact lets customers review, accept, and track agreements with AWS, such as a BAA, in addition to downloading compliance reports.
whyWrong: Config records resource configuration and compliance, not agreements.
Trusted Advisor gives best-practice recommendations, not legal agreements.
Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities, not agreements.

questions.stem: An auditor asks for a record of which IAM principals downloaded individual files from the Amazon S3 bucket that holds a model's training data. The company's trail logs only its default events. What must the company do?
options: Add an AWS Config rule that tracks changes to the bucket's settings
Run Amazon Inspector scans on the bucket to report each file accessed
Enable CloudTrail data events for the objects in the training bucket
Turn on CloudTrail log file validation for the existing trail
questions.explanation: Object-level calls such as GetObject are CloudTrail data events, which trails do not log by default. Turning on data events for the bucket records who read each training file.
whyWrong: Config records resource configuration changes, not object downloads.
Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities; it does not log data access.
Log file validation proves log files were not changed; it does not add object-level events.

questions.stem: A company runs AI workloads in several accounts. Its governance team has chosen a set of resource checks and automatic fixes, such as checks on encryption and logging settings, and wants to deploy and track them as one unit wherever the workloads run. What should it use?
options: An AWS CloudTrail organization trail
An AWS Artifact agreement
An Amazon Inspector scan configuration
An AWS Config conformance pack
questions.explanation: A conformance pack packages AWS Config rules and remediation actions into a single entity that can be deployed in an account and Region or across an organization, with compliance tracking.
whyWrong: A trail records API activity; it does not evaluate resources against rules.
Artifact provides compliance reports and agreements, not checks on resources.
Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities, not configuration rule compliance.

questions.stem: A company's data governance policy for an Amazon Bedrock application has two rules. Overwritten or deleted training files in Amazon S3 must stay recoverable, and model invocation logs sent to Amazon CloudWatch Logs must be deleted automatically after one year. Which two actions meet these rules? (Choose two.)
options: Move the training files to S3 Glacier Deep Archive to lower storage costs
Disable model invocation logging after the first year of operation
Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket that holds the training files
Turn on CloudTrail data events for the training data bucket
Set the retention of the invocation log group to one year
questions.explanation: S3 Versioning keeps every version of an object, so overwritten or deleted files can be restored. CloudWatch Logs keeps log data indefinitely by default, and a log group retention setting deletes events older than the chosen period.
whyWrong: Archiving cuts cost but does not make overwritten or deleted files recoverable.
Turning off logging stops new logs but does not delete the ones already stored.
Data events record access; they cannot restore a deleted file.

questions.stem: A company's AI policy sets minimum quality levels and a regular evaluation schedule for its generative AI assistant. The team then fine-tunes the model, and a manager suggests skipping the next scheduled evaluation because the base model already passed. What does good governance require?
options: Skip evaluation until users report problems, since fine-tuning only adds knowledge
Evaluate it against the same criteria and cadence as the base model
Evaluate only the base model, because the fine-tuned version inherits its results
Replace scheduled evaluation with a one-time review at launch
questions.explanation: Customized and fine-tuned models should meet the same evaluation criteria and cadence as non-customized models, in line with the organization's AI policy.
whyWrong: Customization can change behavior, so waiting for complaints is too late.
A customized model can behave differently and must be tested itself.
Governance calls for periodic review, not a single check.

questions.stem: A company is setting up governance for its generative AI workloads. Which two actions support its governance process? (Choose two.)
options: Name a single workload owner and set minimum performance levels in the AI policy
Let each team define its own evaluation standards so no central policy is needed
Review the model only at launch, because model weights do not change after deployment
Run periodic evaluations against ground truth data, refreshed as usage changes
Keep evaluation results private to the building team to avoid slowing releases
questions.explanation: Governance defines policy, owners, and minimum performance levels, then checks them on a regular cadence against ground truth data that is refreshed as usage changes.
whyWrong: Without a central policy, standards diverge and governance has nothing to enforce.
Inputs and usage change over time, so performance can degrade after launch.
Sharing results with reviewers is part of oversight and transparency.
